## Abstract

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-papillomaviruses are near-ubiquitous skin commensals, yet whether they are transcriptionally active in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) is unsettled. Because standard pipelines discard the non-human reads carrying viral signal, we re-mined `r comma(stats$n_screened)` public human RNA-seq libraries, typing positives and scoring productive infection from late (L1) capsid transcripts, with cell-line provenance, sequencing depth and library chemistry controlled. HPV signal concentrated in non-primary material: cell-line and engineered libraries were five-fold enriched for positivity (*P* < 10⁻⁸), dominated by integrated HPV16/HPV18, whereas primary skin carried HPV at 2–4%. Productive infection was abundant in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (`r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% above a control-calibrated floor). cSCC and actinic keratosis, though sequenced four times more deeply, reached that floor in `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`% of libraries, with median burden six orders of magnitude lower, and were indistinguishable from each other. The deficit was explained neither by depth nor by library chemistry. A minority of primary lesions carried genuine productive gamma- and alpha-HPV infection. Cutaneous HPV is productive in warts but transcriptionally quiet in healthy skin and carcinoma: a trace, non-productive footprint that any account of beta-HPV in skin cancer must accommodate.

**Keywords:** human papillomavirus; beta-papillomavirus; cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma; productive infection; RNA-seq; public data re-mining; contamination
